Exact wording

English (as recorded here)
“All real living is meeting.”
German
“Alles wirkliche Leben ist Begegnung.”

One sentence closing the first part of Ich und Du (1923). English translations diverge sharply: “All real living is meeting” and “All actual life is encounter” are the same German.

Forms in circulation that differ

  • “All real living is meeting.”
  • “All actual life is encounter.”

Attribution notes

The variance here is not a corruption but a genuine split in the English tradition of translating Buber, so two readers citing different renderings of the same German line can both be right about the source and disagree about the words. Buber means a specific kind of relation — the I–Thou encounter, which is not a meeting in the scheduling sense — and the plain English word “meeting” has drifted far from that since the translation was made.

About Martin Buber

Martin Buber (1878–1965) was an Austrian-Jewish philosopher and theologian best known for I and Thou (1923). Active in Zionist cultural politics, Hasidic storytelling, and Bible translation with Franz Rosenzweig, he later taught at Hebrew University.

Interpretation

Buber's sentence is the thesis of I and Thou in miniature. He distinguishes two modes: treating something as an "it" — an object to be classified, used, or studied — and entering into relation with it as a "thou". His claim is that genuine living occurs in the second mode, and that a life organised entirely around the first is diminished even when it is successful. The word "meeting" is deliberate: relation is an event, not a property you possess.

Why it matters

It gives a way to notice the shift: are you dealing with this person, task, or place as something to be managed, or as something you are present to? The difference shows up in attention before it shows up in outcomes.
